title: 4 Top Android Tablets That Outshine the New OLED iPad Mini – BGR Picks 2024
body:
Apple’s much‑anticipated OLED iPad mini is set to hit stores later this year, promising a brighter display, slimmer bezels and the familiar iPad ecosystem that many users rely on for productivity and entertainment. Yet the premium price tag and the closed‑system nature of iOS have prompted a growing segment of shoppers to look beyond Apple’s newest offering. In the Android arena, four tablets stand out for delivering flagship‑level performance, versatile accessories and price points that undercut the iPad mini while still catering to power users. These devices—Samsung’s Galaxy Tab S9 FE, Lenovo’s Tab P12 Pro, Amazon’s refreshed Alexa Tablet line, and the upcoming Xiaomi Pad 6 Pro—provide compelling alternatives for anyone who wants a high‑end tablet without committing to Apple’s ecosystem.

Samsung’s Galaxy Tab S9 FE (Fan Edition) builds on the company’s established reputation for premium tablets, pairing a 10.5‑inch LTPS LCD with a 120 Hz refresh rate and the Snapdragon 8+ Gen 1 processor. The “FE” moniker signals a slightly trimmed feature set—no S‑Pen storage in the body and a modestly lower‑resolution screen—but the device still supports the full S‑Pen, making it a solid choice for note‑taking, sketching and on‑the‑go content creation. Battery life tops out at 12 hours of mixed‑use, and Samsung’s One UI 6.0 offers a seamless multitasking experience with split‑screen and DeX modes that emulate a desktop environment. Priced around $599, the Tab S9 FE undercuts the iPad mini’s expected launch price by roughly $150 while delivering comparable raw horsepower.

Lenovo’s Tab P12 Pro pushes the envelope further with an 12.6‑inch OLED panel that rivals the iPad mini’s new display in brightness and color accuracy. Powered by the Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 chipset, the tablet handles gaming, video editing and AI‑enhanced applications without a hitch. Lenovo’s inclusion of a detachable keyboard and a stylus that magnetically attaches to the rear gives the device a laptop‑like versatility that many Android tablets lack. The tablet also supports Wi‑Fi 6E and optional 5G, ensuring future‑proof connectivity. At $749, the Tab P12 Pro sits in the same price band as Apple’s premium mini but offers a larger screen and a more open software environment, which can be a decisive factor for users who need to run custom apps or multiple user profiles.

Amazon’s latest Alexa Tablet series marks a strategic shift for the e‑commerce giant, moving away from the budget‑focused Fire tablets that have long been relegated to the low‑end market. The new models feature 10.1‑inch LCDs with 1080p resolution, MediaTek Dimensity 900 processors and integrated Alexa voice control that can manage smart‑home devices, stream content and run Android apps via the Amazon Appstore. While the tablets still run a heavily customized version of Android, they now include Google Play compatibility, expanding the app ecosystem dramatically. Pricing starts at $329, positioning the Alexa Tablet as a cost‑effective alternative for families and casual users who want a capable device without the premium price of Apple’s mini. The inclusion of a robust parental‑control suite and a built‑in “Kids Mode” also differentiates it from the iPad mini’s more rigid ecosystem.

Looking ahead, Xiaomi is poised to launch the Pad 6 Pro, a device that could reshape the Android tablet market with its combination of a 120 Hz AMOLED screen, Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 processor and a 5,000 mAh battery that promises up to 14 hours of video playback. Early leaks suggest the tablet will support a magnetic keyboard and stylus, mirroring the productivity‑centric features that have made the iPad mini a favorite among students and professionals. Xiaomi’s aggressive pricing strategy—rumored to be under $600—could make the Pad 6 Pro the most competitively priced flagship tablet on the market, further eroding the iPad mini’s price advantage.

The broader narrative here is not merely about price competition but about the evolving expectations of tablet users. Android manufacturers are increasingly focusing on multitasking capabilities, accessory ecosystems and display technologies that match or exceed Apple’s offerings. Meanwhile, Apple’s control over hardware and software continues to appeal to a loyal base that values seamless integration with macOS, iPhone and Apple Watch. For consumers, the choice now hinges on whether they prioritize ecosystem lock‑in and long‑term software updates, or whether they value flexibility, hardware variety and a lower total cost of ownership.
